milestones.title: Ōta Dōkan builds Edo Castle
milestones.detail: A retainer of the Uesugi clan builds a castle on the former fortified residence of the Edo clan. A small castle town grows beside it along the Hirakawa River.

milestones.title: Tokugawa Ieyasu enters Edo
milestones.detail: After the siege of Odawara, Ieyasu is given the Kantō region and makes the small, run-down castle his base. He begins laying out a castle town and filling in the tidal inlets.

milestones.title: Edo becomes the shogunate's capital
milestones.detail: Ieyasu is appointed shogun and governs Japan from Edo Castle. He orders the daimyo to build out the city, cutting down Kanda hill to fill Hibiya inlet.

milestones.title: Alternate attendance fills Edo with daimyo estates
milestones.detail: The sankin-kōtai system requires every daimyo to keep a residence in Edo. Samurai districts come to occupy about 70 percent of the city's area.

milestones.title: Great Fire of Meireki
milestones.detail: Fire destroys most of Edo, including the castle keep, with a death toll put at around 100,000. The rebuilt city has wider streets and firebreaks and spreads east across the Sumida River.

milestones.title: First regular census; Edo passes one million
milestones.detail: The shogunate's first regular count records 501,394 townspeople. With the uncounted samurai population, historians put the total above one million, among the largest cities in the world.

milestones.title: Edo renamed Tokyo, the Eastern Capital
milestones.detail: After the fall of the shogunate, Edo is renamed Tokyo on 3 September 1868 and the emperor moves from Kyoto. Edo Castle becomes the Imperial Palace.

milestones.title: Japan's first railway reaches Tokyo
milestones.detail: The country's first railway opens between Shimbashi in Tokyo and Yokohama.

milestones.title: Tokyo City established
milestones.detail: The 15 wards of the old city are incorporated as Tokyo City on 1 May 1889, within Tokyo Prefecture.

milestones.title: Great Kantō earthquake
milestones.detail: The earthquake of 1 September 1923 and the fires that follow kill an estimated 105,000 people and level much of the low city. Rebuilding shifts construction from timber and brick to reinforced concrete.

milestones.title: First subway opens between Ueno and Asakusa
milestones.detail: The first section of what is now the Ginza Line opens on 30 December 1927, the first underground railway built outside Europe and the Americas.

milestones.title: Greater Tokyo: 82 towns and villages absorbed
milestones.detail: Tokyo City annexes 82 surrounding municipalities on 1 October 1932, growing from 15 to 35 wards and reaching roughly the extent of today's 23 special wards.

milestones.title: Tokyo Metropolis created
milestones.detail: Tokyo City and Tokyo Prefecture are merged into a single Tokyo Metropolis (Tōkyō-to) on 1 July 1943.

milestones.title: Firebombing destroys half the city
milestones.detail: The air raid of 9-10 March 1945 burns out two-fifths of the city, destroys more than 276,000 buildings and kills about 100,000 civilians. The metropolis's population falls by half within a year.

milestones.title: Olympic Games and the first Shinkansen
milestones.detail: Tokyo hosts the first Olympic Games held in Asia. The Tōkaidō Shinkansen to Osaka and the Shuto Expressway open the same year.

milestones.title: Kasumigaseki Building starts the skyscraper era
milestones.detail: With the 31-metre building height limit relaxed, the Kasumigaseki Building becomes Tokyo's first modern skyscraper. Towers over 200 metres follow in West Shinjuku in the 1970s.

milestones.title: Second Tokyo Olympics
milestones.detail: The 2020 Summer Olympics, postponed by the COVID-19 pandemic, are held from 23 July to 8 August 2021. Tokyo is the first Asian city to host the Games twice.

notes: Start date: 1457 is the conventional founding date (Ōta Dōkan's castle). The site was fortified earlier by the Edo clan around the end of the 12th century, but no dated record fixes that; Sensō-ji in Asakusa has a traditional founding of 628/645, which is temple legend, and its first documentary mention is 1181. Population before 1872: the shogunate only ever counted townspeople (about 500,000 from 1721, peaking at 575,091 in 1853); samurai, retainers and clergy were not counted, so every total is a scholarly estimate and they disagree widely. This file uses the Japanese estimates (Saitō 1984, Kitō 1989) of about 1.0-1.2 million for 1721-1850; Chandler (1987) assumes a much smaller samurai population and gives only 685,000-788,000 for the same period, and other Japanese estimates run to 1.3 million. No estimate was found for 1457-1599, so the series starts with Chandler's figure for 1600. Population 1872-1945 is the official Tokyo Metropolitan Government series for Tokyo Prefecture (later Metropolis), not the city proper; the prefecture was enlarged in the 1890s. The UN series from 1950 covers the whole multi-prefecture urban agglomeration and is far larger than the prefecture figure, so expect a step at 1950. Landmarks: the Edo Castle keep height (51 m) and the Sensō-ji pagoda height (podium plus tower) come from Wikipedia rather than a survey, and are marked estimated; coordinates for the Zōjō-ji gate and the Sensō-ji pagoda are those of the temple compounds, accurate to roughly 100 m. Left out for lack of a consistent sourced height: Ryōunkaku (the 1890 Asakusa twelve-storey tower; sources give 52 m and 68.58 m), Tokyo Station (1914), the Kan'ei-ji pagoda and Meiji Shrine. The Japan National Stadium (2019) was also left out because no height was found.
